overview.title: Parsing the Jena data and plotting the temperature
overview.main_topic: Finishing the CSV-to-NumPy parsing of the Jena climate dataset and taking a first look at the temperature timeseries at two timescales (full eight years and first 10 days).
overview.central_idea: Each of the 420,551 CSV lines becomes one row of a (420551, 14) float array plus one entry of a temperature vector; plotting that vector reveals a strong yearly cycle, and zooming to 1,440 points (10 days at 144 points per day) sets up the look at daily cycles.
overview.importance: Every model in chapter 13 is trained on exactly these two arrays, raw_data and temperature. Looking at the plots before modeling is how you discover the periodicity that later explains why the problem is easy at month scale and hard at day scale (p.379).
learning_objectives: Explain what the parsing loop does with each CSV line and why column 0 (Date Time) is dropped.
State the shapes of raw_data and temperature after Listing 13.2.
Read Figure 13.1 and identify the yearly periodicity across eight years.
Derive the 144 samples per day and 1,440 samples per 10 days from the 10-minute sampling interval.
Use matplotlib's plt.plot to make a quick exploratory plot of a 1D NumPy array.
prerequisites: Listing 13.1 (p.377): reading the CSV into lines and header
Basic NumPy: np.zeros, row assignment, slicing
Basic Python string handling: split, list comprehensions, enumerate

summary:
This page completes **Listing 13.2** (begun on p.377) and adds two quick exploratory plots.

**Parsing.** After `temperature = np.zeros((len(lines),))` on p.377, the code allocates `raw_data = np.zeros((len(lines), len(header) - 1))`, a 420,551 x 14 array: one row per timestep and one column per weather quantity, the `-1` removing the "Date Time" column. The loop then walks over every line, splits it on commas, drops the first field (the date string) with `[1:]`, and converts the remaining 14 fields to floats. Column 1 of those values, which is `T (degC)` in the header of p.377, is stored in `temperature[i]`; the full list of 14 values, temperature included, is stored in row `i` of `raw_data`, as the two callouts say.

**Full-range plot.** Listing 13.3 imports `pyplot` and plots `temperature` against its index. Figure 13.1 shows values from roughly -20 to about 35 degrees Celsius with eight clear yearly humps: the data covers eight years (2009 to 2016, p.376). The x axis is the timestep index, not a date.

**First 10 days.** Because one record is taken every 10 minutes, a day contains $24 \times 6 = 144$ records, so 10 days are $1{,}440$ records. Listing 13.4 plots `temperature[:1440]`; that plot (Figure 13.2) is on p.379, where the book discusses daily periodicity.

Note: the text calls the figures "Figure 10.1" and "Figure 10.2", while the captions say Figure 13.1 and 13.2. The numbers seem to be left over from the previous edition.

paragraphs.excerpt: Figure 10.1 shows the plot of temperature (in degrees Celsius) over time.
paragraphs.what_it_says: The plot of the temperature column over the whole dataset (made by Listing 13.3 and printed as Figure 13.1) clearly shows yearly periodicity, and the data spans eight years.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each hump in Figure 13.1 is one year: temperatures rise to around 30-35 degC in summer and drop below zero, sometimes to -20 degC, in winter. Eight such cycles over about 420,000 timesteps correspond to the 2009-2016 range described on p.376. Within each hump the curve is thick and jagged because of shorter-term variation: day and night cycles and weather changes.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Seeing a strong, regular seasonal cycle tells you that part of the signal is very predictable at long timescales. On p.379 the book uses this to argue that predicting next month's average would be easy, while day-scale prediction looks much more chaotic. This is the core difficulty of the chapter.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Plotting a raw series before modeling is a basic exploratory step. It shows periodicity, trends, outliers and gaps, all of which affect how you split and normalize the data and which baselines make sense.

terminology.meaning: A pattern that repeats at a regular interval, here one year.
One row of the dataset, one 10-minute measurement.

connections: p.376: the dataset is the 2009-2016 subset of the Jena weather station records, with 14 quantities every 10 minutes.
p.379: the NOTE on periodicity over multiple timescales (daily, weekly, yearly).
p.383: the commonsense baseline uses the fact that temperature is fairly continuous.

paragraphs.excerpt: Figure 10.2 shows a more narrow plot of the first 10 days
paragraphs.what_it_says: A second plot zooms in on the first 10 days of temperature. Because there is one record every 10 minutes, there are 24 x 6 = 144 data points per day, so 10 days are the first 1,440 points plotted in Listing 13.4.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The arithmetic turns a time span into an index range: 6 records per hour x 24 hours = 144 per day, and 144 x 10 = 1,440. The slice `temperature[:1440]` is therefore exactly the first 10 days, starting at 2009-01-01 (a winter month, as p.379 notes).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Converting between wall-clock time and number of timesteps comes up throughout the chapter. On p.381, `sampling_rate = 6` keeps one point per hour, `sequence_length = 120` covers five days of hourly points, and the 24-hour-ahead target is defined through `delay`. Getting comfortable with the 6-per-hour and 144-per-day factors here makes those parameters easy to read.
paragraphs.technical_idea: At 10-minute resolution, one day is 144 steps and one year is about 144 x 365.25 = 52,596 steps, so eight years give about 420,768 steps. That is close to the 420,551 lines reported on p.377. The small difference suggests a few missing records (inference, not stated in the book).

concepts.name: Timeseries
concepts.definition: Data obtained by measurements at regular intervals, where the order of the measurements carries information.
concepts.intuition: A row of numbers where row i+1 happens 10 minutes after row i, so neighbouring rows are strongly related.
concepts.technical: Here the series is multivariate: 14 channels (pressure, temperature, humidity, wind, ...) sampled every 10 minutes, stored as a (timesteps, features) array.
concepts.significance: Unlike shuffled image or text datasets, order matters. That affects how you split data (chronologically, p.379) and which architectures work (RNNs, p.388).
concepts.example: raw_data[i] is the 14-value weather record for timestep i; temperature[i] is the temperature at that moment.
concepts.misconception: A timeseries is not just a table of independent rows; shuffling it before splitting would leak future information into training.

concepts.name: Periodicity
concepts.definition: Regular repetition of a pattern over time, at one or more timescales.
concepts.intuition: Summer and winter repeat every year; day and night repeat every day.
concepts.technical: In Figure 13.1 the dominant period is one year (about 52,600 timesteps at 10-minute resolution); the daily period (144 timesteps) appears in the 10-day zoom on p.379.
concepts.significance: Strong periodicity makes long-horizon averages predictable and gives simple baselines something to exploit; residual short-term variation is what makes daily forecasting hard.
concepts.example: Eight yearly humps across eight years of data in Figure 13.1.
concepts.misconception: A visible yearly cycle does not mean tomorrow's temperature is easy to predict; the day-to-day variation is much less regular.

concepts.name: Exploratory plotting
concepts.definition: Visualizing raw data before modeling to understand its structure.
concepts.intuition: Look at the data before you trust a model to.
concepts.technical: plt.plot(range(len(x)), x) gives a quick line plot of a 1D array against its index; slicing zooms in on a time window.
concepts.significance: Reveals scale, cycles, outliers and the regime (winter start) of the data, which inform normalization and baselines.
concepts.example: Plotting temperature[:1440] to inspect the first 10 days.
concepts.misconception: The x axis in these plots is the row index, not a calendar date.

code.title: Parsing the data (continued from p.377)
code.original_code:
raw_data = np.zeros((len(lines), len(header) - 1))

for i, line in enumerate(lines):
    values = [float(x) for x in line.split(",")[1:]]
    temperature[i] = values[1]
    raw_data[i, :] = values[:]
code.what_it_does: Allocates the feature array and fills it, along with the temperature array allocated on p.377, by parsing every CSV line into floats. The first two lines of the listing (`import numpy as np` and `temperature = np.zeros((len(lines),))`) are on p.377.

line_explanations.explanation: Creates a zero array of shape (420551, 14): one row per line, and len(header) - 1 columns because the "Date Time" column is not stored.
enumerate gives both the row index i and the raw text line.
Splits the line on commas, drops field 0 (the date string) with [1:], and converts the 14 remaining fields to Python floats.
values[1] is the second non-date column, T (degC) in the header of p.377 (values[0] is p (mbar)). Callout: 'We store column 1 in the temperature array.'
Copies all 14 values into row i of raw_data. Callout: 'We store all columns (including the temperature) in the raw_data array.'

code.inputs_outputs: Input: lines (list of CSV strings without the header) and header (list of 15 column names) from Listing 13.1. Output: temperature with shape (420551,) and raw_data with shape (420551, 14), both float64.
code.algorithm: A row-by-row parse into preallocated arrays.
code.theory_link: raw_data holds the model's input features and temperature holds the target. Because temperature is also a column of raw_data, the model can see past temperatures, which is the most informative feature for forecasting future ones.

parameters.role: Selects the T (degC) column as the forecasting target.

pitfalls: The file ends with a newline, so data.split("\n") on p.377 can produce a trailing empty string. If it does, float('') raises a ValueError; a robust version filters empty lines (not discussed in the book).
values[1] is the index after dropping the date. In the original CSV columns, the temperature is column 2.
A Python loop over 420k lines is slow-ish (seconds). np.loadtxt or pandas.read_csv would be faster, but the explicit loop is clearer for teaching.

# AI-written alternative (not from the book)
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("jena_climate_2009_2016.csv")

print(raw_data.shape, temperature.shape)  # (420551, 14) (420551,)

deeper.title: Tracing one CSV line through the loop
deeper.body:
Suppose a line reads `01.01.2009 00:10:00,996.52,-8.02,265.4,...` (format as in the Jena CSV; the values are illustrative).

1. `line.split(",")` gives `['01.01.2009 00:10:00', '996.52', '-8.02', '265.4', ...]` (15 strings).
2. `[1:]` drops the date, leaving 14 strings.
3. The list comprehension converts them: `[996.52, -8.02, 265.4, ...]`.
4. `values[1]` is `-8.02`, the temperature in degC, stored in `temperature[i]`.
5. All 14 floats are stored in `raw_data[i, :]`.

So `raw_data[:, 1]` and `temperature` hold the same numbers.

deeper.title: Why keep temperature both as a target and as a feature?
deeper.body: The forecasting task (p.380) is to predict the temperature 24 hours after a five-day window. The inputs are the window of `raw_data`, and the target is a later value of `temperature`. Keeping the temperature among the inputs gives the model the past values of the quantity it has to predict. The commonsense baseline on p.383 relies on that alone (it predicts that the temperature in 24 hours equals the current one). Removing it would make the task much harder. A separate `temperature` vector just makes target lookup simple when building datasets with `timeseries_dataset_from_array` (p.381).

deeper.title: Reading timescales off the index
deeper.body:
At 10-minute sampling:

| span | timesteps |
|---|---|
| 1 hour | 6 |
| 1 day | 144 |
| 5 days | 720 (120 hourly points after `sampling_rate=6`, p.381) |
| 10 days | 1,440 |
| 1 year | about 52,596 |
| 8 years | about 420,768 (dataset: 420,551) |

In Figure 13.1, the peaks near x = 25k, 80k, 130k, ... are about 52k apart, one per summer.

questions.question: What are the shapes of raw_data and temperature after Listing 13.2 runs, and why does raw_data have len(header) - 1 columns?
questions.answer: raw_data is (420551, 14) and temperature is (420551,). The header has 15 names; the Date Time column is discarded, leaving 14.
questions.explanation: len(lines) = 420,551 (p.377); [1:] drops the date field from every line, so 14 numeric values remain per row.

questions.question: Inside the loop, which quantity does values[1] contain?
questions.explanation: values excludes the date, so values[0] is p (mbar) and values[1] is T (degC), the column the callout says is stored in temperature. The date was removed by [1:], and Tpot is values[2].

questions.question: The data is recorded every 10 minutes. How many records cover 10 days, and roughly how many cover one year?
questions.answer: 1,440 for 10 days; about 52,600 for one year.
questions.explanation: 6 per hour x 24 = 144 per day (p.378); x 10 = 1,440. Beyond the book: 144 x 365.25 is about 52,596, and eight years give about 420,768, consistent with 420,551 lines.

questions.question: What does Figure 13.1 reveal about the data, and what does it not reveal?
questions.answer: It shows a strong yearly cycle repeated over eight years and the overall range (about -20 to 35 degC). It does not show daily structure, which is hidden by the density of 420k points; that requires the 10-day zoom.
questions.explanation: The book highlights yearly periodicity here and turns to daily periodicity with Figure 13.2 on p.379.

questions.question: According to the callouts, what does raw_data contain?
questions.explanation: The callout reads 'We store all columns (including the temperature) in the raw_data array'. The date is dropped by [1:], so it is not 15 columns, and temperature is not excluded.

questions.question: Which figure is the text calling 'Figure 10.1', and why might the number differ?
questions.answer: Figure 13.1, the full-range temperature plot. The '10.x' numbering likely comes from the previous edition, where timeseries forecasting was chapter 10.
questions.explanation: The caption on the page reads Figure 13.1; the reference in the text does not match it.

questions.explanation: Each day is 144 timesteps, so day d starts at index 144*d.
